episodes.title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls
episodes.speaker: Brad Beasley
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brad Beasley, a podiatrist (DPM), presents an interactive lecture on diabetic foot care for family medicine residents. He emphasizes the high morbidity of diabetic foot ulcers, the critical role of neuropathy in wound formation, and the often-missed diagnosis of Charcot neuroarthropathy. Practical advice includes checking shoe fit as a simple intervention, recognizing that diabetics may not mount a typical infectious response, and stressing strict non-weight-bearing for Charcot. The talk aims to provide immediately actionable clinical pearls for the office setting.
key_points: DPMs (Doctors of Podiatric Medicine) complete a medical-school-based curriculum with early specialization in lower extremity care, followed by a 3-year residency.
Diabetic foot ulcers have high morbidity and mortality, often worse than many cancers, yet receive less attention.
Neuropathy is the primary contributor to diabetic foot wounds, as it masks pain from injury.
Charcot neuroarthropathy presents as a swollen, red, painless foot in a neuropathic diabetic; it is frequently missed and requires immediate offloading.
X-ray showing bone fragmentation or dislocation is key for diagnosing Charcot; MRI may help differentiate from osteomyelitis.
In diabetics with infection, white blood cell count and left shift may not be elevated due to impaired cellular response.
Over 90% of adults wear the wrong shoe size; shoes should allow about half an inch of space beyond the longest toe.
Simple shoe-fit correction can resolve forefoot pain, nail thickening, and skin issues in neuropathic patients.
Diabetics should remove shoes and socks at every visit, even for non-foot complaints, to facilitate early detection of pathology.
Charcot neuroarthropathy progression takes 6-9 months; strict non-weight-bearing for at least 3 months is critical to prevent foot collapse.
Foot infection is the number one reason a diabetic is hospitalized.
An A1c below 8 is a threshold to reduce lower extremity complications.

episodes.title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26
episodes.speaker: Cyr
episodes.abstract: This lecture, delivered by Dr. Cyr, covers the clinical distinction of migraine from other headache types, emphasizing the POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile quality, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling intensity) for diagnosis. Practical management strategies include headache diaries (with an app called Migraine Buddy), early use of NSAIDs or triptans, and a stepped approach to rescue therapy. The speaker also highlights the risk of medication overuse and shares a personal experience with monthly injectable preventive therapy (Ajovy) to illustrate the value of prophylaxis.
key_points: Migraine is a recurring headache lasting 4–72 hours, typically unilateral, moderate-to-severe, aggravated by routine activity, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia.
The POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling) helps increase diagnostic probability for migraine.

Key history questions include triggers (sleep, caffeine, missed meals, weather), red-flag symptoms (Snoop mnemonic: Systemic, Neurologic, Older age >50, Onset sudden, Pattern change), and what the patient has tried at home.
Headache diaries, especially using a free app like Migraine Buddy, help identify triggers and track medication response; they are a recommended tool for patients.
First-line rescue therapy includes acetaminophen, NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen), and aspirin; triptans are more effective when combined with naproxen.
Triptans should be taken early at headache onset; increasing the dose of the same triptan does not generally improve efficacy—if one fails, try a different triptan.
Medication overuse headache is a common pitfall: limit triptan use to <10 days per month to avoid rebound headaches.
Preventive therapy (e.g., monthly injectable anti-CGRP like Ajovy) can dramatically reduce migraine frequency, as illustrated by the speaker’s personal improvement after six months.
Non-pharmacologic measures (dark room, rest, ice/heat packs, hydration) are important adjuncts and should be reinforced with patients.
Recognizing prodromal features (e.g., yawning, fatigue, neck pain) can help patients initiate treatment earlier and potentially reduce attack severity.
Medication overuse limits: analgesics ≤3 days/week, triptans ≤2 days/week or 8 days/month.
Indications for prophylaxis: frequent headaches, medication overuse, interference with daily activities, patient preference.

pearls.text: In diabetics with infection, you cannot rely on elevated white blood cell count or left shift because high blood sugar impairs the cellular immune response.
pearls.verbatim: as you know with diabetics, they don't mount the same cellular response. So you don't always get a elevated white count or left shift with infection in diabetics, so you can't always use that as an indicator.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: When a neuropathic diabetic presents with a swollen, red, painless foot, suspect Charcot neuroarthropathy; get them off the foot immediately with strict non-weight-bearing.
pearls.verbatim: So anytime you have numbness in your feet or legs, you can get these micro traumas in your feet. You don't feel it, and your feet just collapse. ... get the patient off of the foot immediately.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For Charcot neuroarthropathy, patients must be 100% non-weight-bearing for at least three months, sometimes six, to halt fragmentation and prevent catastrophic wounds.
pearls.verbatim: They're a 100% non weight bearing ideally for at least three months, sometimes six. If we don't take care of that, then they develop.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Over 90% of adults wear the wrong shoe size. Check that there is about half an inch of space between the longest toe and the end of the shoe, and that toes are not compressed together.
pearls.verbatim: over ninety percent of adults wear the wrong size shoe. ... You should have about almost half an inch of distance between the end of your toe and the end of the shoe, and you shouldn't be putting your toes together.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: When a diabetic presents with thick nails or chronic forefoot pain that hasn't responded to treatment, consider that their shoes may be one to two sizes too small, causing repetitive rubbing.
pearls.verbatim: They come in with, like, I've been to a lot of doctors, and my nails are thick. They won't get any better with all these expensive prescriptions. ... realizing they're wearing their shoes at least a full, maybe two sizes too small.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For a neuropathic diabetic with a swollen, red foot but no wound, Charcot is the most likely diagnosis; D-dimer is not helpful for ruling out DVT because inflammation from Charcot elevates it.
pearls.verbatim: the key, though, if you see that change in the foot and there's no wound, probably a Charcot. ... D dimer can be helpful in a pinch. ... But when they've got inflammation from Charcot, it's gonna be high anyway, so it doesn't really rule it out.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Always have diabetic patients remove their shoes and socks at every visit, regardless of the chief complaint, to inspect for early foot problems.
pearls.verbatim: always get in the habit when you have a diabetic. Even if they're coming in just for a A1c check or to look at something else, have them take their shoes and socks off.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: When Charcot is suspected, get an X-ray; if you see bone fragmentation or dislocation, the patient needs strict non-weight-bearing and a boot or specialty referral.
pearls.verbatim: So if you see a foot X-ray that... Where the bones are fragmenting or looking like they're shifting, get the patient off of the foot immediately. Obviously, if you see these symptoms come into the office, you're gonna wanna look at, is there infection? Is there a DVT? Things like that. But Charcot is often missed. And so it's getting off the foot, putting them in a boot, getting them to see us or if you know an ortho that does.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Charcot neuroarthropathy can allow patients to walk on a collapsing foot without pain; they will think your concern is overblown, but early offloading prevents limb loss.
pearls.verbatim: a lot of them are ambulating thinking nothing's wrong. They can't feel it. You try to get them off of it ASAP so the fragmentation stops.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Cover open wounds with a small kitchen trash bag or shower cover to prevent shower water from entering the wound and causing infection.
pearls.verbatim: If they have an open wound, just tell them to put a bag over the foot. Shower water going down across their body, all that dirty water goes up into that hole in the bottom of their foot, and that's how we set up a bad infection.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Obtain a deep swab culture before starting antibiotics; poke the swab into the wound and move it around inside, avoiding a quick smear, and debride tissue if possible.
pearls.verbatim: It's best to get a little bit of tissue on it if you can. So either you can... I mean, the basic thing is just to get a deep swab. Just poke it into the wound and move it around all inside the wound. Don't just do a quick smear.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Do not start broad-spectrum antibiotics like Zosyn before culturing; once antibiotics are given, cultures may not grow anything.
pearls.verbatim: Too often, stuff comes in through the ED, and they immediately start, like, bag of Zosyn, and they're hammering it with all these heavy medications. They didn't get a culture. So at that point, we can't culture. Nothing's gonna grow well when it's hammered with all these antibiotics.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Use hypochlorous acid at 200 ppm for wound cleaning; it is nontoxic, antimicrobial, and may improve tissue perfusion without slowing healing.
pearls.verbatim: Two hundred parts per million is the concentration for skin use. Four hundred parts per million is usually used for disinfection of the surface. Either is safe to put on your body.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Never mix bleach with Dawn dish soap or similar products; this can create chlorine gas and cause respiratory distress.
pearls.verbatim: Never mixed those two things together. So it depends if you... If they start mixing it with soap or things like that, they can get that because we don't know those things until you try. So don't try it.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For diabetic shoe programs, the physician must sign a certifying statement and submit notes; any error in address or phone number can lead to denial.
pearls.verbatim: They need a prescription from a podiatrist or their physician, and they need their physician to sign a certifying statement. Whoever's treating their diabetes, to sign a certifying statement that a diabetic shoe is a benefit to them, and they have to submit notes.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: An A1c below 8 is the threshold to reduce lower extremity complications; higher levels increase risk of foot problems and retinopathy.
pearls.verbatim: we want a little much lower than eight, but eight seems to be the threshold where bad things... A lot of bad things start happening, especially lower extremity.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Smoking causes vasoconstriction within seconds and lasts throughout the smoking period; patients who smoke a pack a day have essentially no blood flow to skin and legs and will not heal until they stop.
pearls.verbatim: That causes vasoconstriction in about four seconds after you start smoking, and it lasts the entire time and a little bit after they're smoking. So if they're doing a pack a day, they pretty much have no blood flow to their skin and their legs all the time. So they won't heal until they stop smoking.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Every time a patient steps on an open wound, they add days to healing by crushing fibroblasts under 100-400 pounds of pressure, preventing any chance of healing.
pearls.verbatim: every time they step on an open wound, they're literally adding a day or two to their healing with them to realize that they're killing those fibroblasts that are trying to grow across because you add a 100 to 400 pounds onto that wound, it'll just crush everything, so there's no chance of healing.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: A knee walker (available on Amazon for ~$100) is an easy offloading device that allows patients to keep weight off the wound while ambulating.
pearls.verbatim: The easiest thing that's available now is a knee walker. You can get them on Amazon for a $100.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For venous wounds, compression is essential; even a couple layers of ACE wraps up the leg can reduce congestion and allow healing.
pearls.verbatim: Pace wounds, you gotta do compression. So whether that's as simple if you're in the field or at a rural clinic, even just doing a couple layers of ACE wraps up the leg, that's a basic way of getting compression until you reduce that congestion in the tissue.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Toe-brachial index is more beneficial than ankle-brachial index because the toe arteries are less affected by hardening.
pearls.verbatim: Tobrachial index is actually a lot more beneficial than an ankle brachial index because of less hardening of the arteries and the.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: A transcutaneous oxygen measurement (TcPO2) above 40 mmHg indicates healing potential; lower values require vascular intervention.
pearls.verbatim: In general, you want above 40 millimeters of mercury pressure on a TcPO2. That tells you you can heal at least 30 At that point, you have a chance. If it's lower than that, you've gotta send them for intervention.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Arterial ultrasound is better than ABI; focus on waveforms (triphasic, biphasic, monophasic) rather than just presence of flow.
pearls.verbatim: Just an arterial ultrasound is better than an ABI. So it's part of the study, but you're more interested in the waveforms than is there actually flow. We'll classify it as triphasic, biphasic, or monophasic flow.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Screen for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with simple tests: thumb can fold down to forearm, elbows/knees hyperextend, skin on neck can be pulled out a couple inches.
pearls.verbatim: Can you fold your thumb down on your forearm? And if they just flatten it down on... Yeah. Everyone's checking that. Or they can, you know, hyperextend their elbows re... Real easier, put their knees in direct or bottom. Those are the easiest things to look where you can have them stretch your skin on your neck. That's another thing. If they could pull it out a couple inches, that's not a... That's not normal.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For superficial wounds with little drainage, use a fabric band-aid; never use plastic band-aids on feet because they cause maceration.
pearls.verbatim: If it's superficial and not draining a lot, they could put fabric Band Aid on. You never want people to put plastic Band Aids on feet, macerate. So fabric Band Aid.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Silver-impregnated dressings like Aquacel Ag or Acticoat can be left in place for 5-7 days because the fibers absorb moisture and silver controls bacteria.
pearls.verbatim: You can get silver impregnated dressings like Aquacel Ag. I should... Like, Acticoat is another one that has silver in it. You can leave those in place for five to seven days because they need the fibers to absorb moisture, and the silver keeps it back.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Culture wounds if they appear infected (purulent drainage, odor, redness, swelling) or if no progress after a few weeks; treat colonized bacteria with oral antibiotics cautiously in diabetics with kidney disease.
pearls.verbatim: If it looks infected, I'll culture it, or if it's chronic, I'll culture it. So if I'm look... If I see drainage that's not just regular serosanguineous drainage, it's pralent or an odor, I'll culture it. Redness, swelling, or if it's just we're not getting any progress over a few weeks, I'll culture it to see if it's colonized.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For foot pain, recommend a shoe that does not flex in the midfoot; a stiff shank reduces stress on tendons, ligaments, and arthritic joints.
pearls.verbatim: you want a shoe that doesn't flex a lot. Okay? If they're having a lot of foot pain, that's an easy thing to do.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For plantar fasciitis, the number one intervention is a stiff-shank shoe, not expensive custom insoles.
pearls.verbatim: Plantar fasciitis, number one thing to think about is just a stiff shank shoe.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: PowerStep over-the-counter insoles are effective and affordable ($45–55) and can be obtained at running stores or podiatry offices.
pearls.verbatim: PowerStep are a great one. If you're looking for something for people to get that's very comfortable.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Cellulitis without a wound in a swollen leg is often non-infectious inflammation due to edema; antibiotics are unnecessary—compression and elevation are key.
pearls.verbatim: if there's no wound and it's just a lot of swelling, then, you know, I wouldn't put them on antibiotics. They just need compression and elevation.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Home pneumatic compression pumps are now available on Amazon for a few hundred dollars and can help patients manage lymphedema at home.
pearls.verbatim: There's pneumatic on Amazon. You can get pneumatic pumps now. It used to be something that cost, like, $5,000. For a couple $100, you can get the pneumatic air pumps that kind of milk the legs.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For fungal toenails, have patients file nails weekly with a disposable emery board after a shower, then apply over-the-counter Tinactin or Aeronal.
pearls.verbatim: We have them start doing weekly filing of their nails to thin them down. Daily, they apply... Tinactin.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Oral terbinafine has only a 70–80% cure rate and a 90% recurrence rate, plus liver toxicity risk; it is usually not worth prescribing.
pearls.verbatim: terbinafine too is only about a seventy to eighty percent cure rate, but it's a ninety percent recurrence rate.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: In diabetics, thick fungal nails cause pressure on the nail bed and distal phalanx, leading to wounds, cellulitis, and osteomyelitis.
pearls.verbatim: for diabetics, it's dangerous because they'll get thick. That creates pressure on the nail bed. Can get wounds and infection... a lot of osteomyelitis of toes just from really thick nails
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Disinfect the inside of shoes with a Lysol wipe to prevent reinfection of nails after treatment for onychomycosis.
pearls.verbatim: disinfect their shoes because fungus is in the shoes. So take a Lysol wipe or wipe wipe out the inside of the shoe.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: For arthritic big toe or turf toe, the shoe should be rigid even at the toe-flex area to prevent painful motion.
pearls.verbatim: someone has terrible big toe arthritis, you want a rigid shoe that doesn't flex at all. And a young person, it'd be like a turf toe injury. You want a stiff sole shoe.
pearls.speaker: Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Use the POUND mnemonic to quickly screen for migraine in a patient with headache: Pulsatile quality, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling intensity.
pearls.verbatim: p, pulsatile quality. O, one day in duration or it's a long time, u, unilateral, thin, nausea or vomiting, and d, disabling intensity.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Ask about activity tolerance: 'If I told you to run around the clinic, would you feel the same, better, or worse?' Migraine worsens with routine physical activity.
pearls.verbatim: if I told you to go run around this clinic, would you feel the same, better, or worse? And it's like, when I have a migraine, you... Like, mm-mm.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Triptans are more effective when combined with naproxen; take naproxen and a caffeinated drink at headache onset, then take the triptan only if still symptomatic after one hour.
pearls.verbatim: Take the naproxen and drink a Coke beginning of your headache and, like, get in a dark room and rest. If in an hour you're still having that headache, take the triptan.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: If one triptan at the standard dose does not work, do not increase the dose; instead, try a different triptan.
pearls.verbatim: If fifty is not working on one triptan, try a different triptan. Don't go to a 100. It's not like an SSRI.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Limit triptan use to avoid rebound headaches — the speaker's personal experience of 20 triptans per month was identified as excessive and contributed to medication overuse headache.
pearls.verbatim: I was probably taking twenty triptans a month. That's bad... and you're having rebound headaches.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Common migraine triggers include stress, lack of sleep, missed meals, weather changes, neck pain, bright sun, dehydration, caffeine (too much or too little), processed foods, and hormone changes like menses.
pearls.verbatim: Stress, lack of sleep. I woke up two hours late. Is that changing how I'm living my life? Yes. Interrupted sleep... Depressed mood. Anxiety. Skip a meal. Very variable weather. Storm... Humidity above 80% also... Neck pain, alcohol, bright, sun, or dehydration... Caffeine, so, like, too little or too much.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Injectable anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies (e.g., Ajovy) are effective preventive options — the speaker's migraine frequency dramatically improved after five to six months of monthly injections.
pearls.verbatim: I started Ajovy... Ajovy is an injectable medicine. To prevent migraine, you take it once a month... after five months... it's, like, so much better.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: During a migraine attack, non-pharmacologic relief methods (dark room, rest, ice pack, heat pack, hydration) should be tried alongside medication.
pearls.verbatim: dark room rest, go down to meditation, staying indoors, ice packs. Also, heat packs is there. Heating pad. Food, caffeine, hot shower, full shower, drink water.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Limit analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) to three days per week and triptans to two days per week or eight days per month to prevent medication overuse headache.
pearls.verbatim: for analgesics, so acetaminophen and NSAIDs, three days per week, days per month. For triptans combined with triptans, other medicine, two days per week or eight days per month.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: If a patient is taking more than the recommended limits of acute headache medications, you need to intervene.
pearls.verbatim: if they're taking more than this, then you need to intervene
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Give a triptan a fair chance—try it at least six times before concluding it doesn't work, and ensure the patient takes it at the beginning of the headache.
pearls.verbatim: give it a fair chance and make sure, like, someone's taking it at the beginning of their headache.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Sumatriptan has the highest side effect profile among triptans; rizatriptan has a low side effect profile and works faster and better.
pearls.verbatim: the sumatriptan that we have, my neurologist told me it has the highest side effect profile of all the other triptans. So we had rizatriptan, and she said that's very good. It has a very low side effect profile, and it, like, works faster and better.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: During a migraine, go into a cold, dark room to rest.
pearls.verbatim: you need to go into your room and, like, make it cold and dark
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Educate patients about medication overuse headache; some headaches may actually be rebound from withdrawal of acute medications.
pearls.verbatim: some of the headaches she's having might actually rebound from withdrawal from the day Absolutely. Prescription.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Set a goal to reduce acute medication use gradually, e.g., from 12 to 6 triptans per month.
pearls.verbatim: set a goal... maybe if your goal is 12 and eventually your goal is, like, six a month.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Topiramate (Topamax) should not be used in women of childbearing age due to teratogenicity.
pearls.verbatim: Topamax... you should not put someone on who's, like, of childbearing age.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: CGRP antagonists are a good option for patients with significant nausea or vomiting during migraines because the gut has many CGRP receptors.
pearls.verbatim: CGRP would be good for me because I have significant nausea with my headaches and occasionally vomiting... your gut is a major one of them.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Insurance often requires trying one or two other preventatives before covering a CGRP antagonist.
pearls.verbatim: insurance usually wants you to try one or two other preventative medications before you
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Frovatriptan is good for menstrual migraines due to its long half-life; take it every day of your period, but be aware of a reliable rebound headache the day after.
pearls.verbatim: frovatriptan, good for menstrual migraines. Very long acting. Every day of your period. And then for me, I had a reliable rebound headache the day after.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Magnesium and triptans in moderation can be considered during pregnancy, though evidence is limited.
pearls.verbatim: magnesium... some evidence that triptans in moderation can be used during pregnancy.
pearls.speaker: Cyr
